title: Ten simple rules for the computational modeling of behavioral data
institution: eLife (Review Article, Neuroscience); authors at the University of Arizona and the University of California, Berkeley
description: Review article giving ten rules, as unnumbered section headings, for computational modelling of behavioural data: design a good experiment; design good models; simulate; fit the parameters (maximum likelihood); check parameter recovery; check model recovery (confusion and inversion matrices, BIC); run the experiment and analyse the data model-independently; validate the winning model by simulation; analyse the winning model; report. Illustrated with a two-armed bandit example (random responding with bias, noisy win-stay-lose-shift, Rescorla-Wagner with softmax, choice kernel, Rescorla-Wagner plus choice kernel; T = 1000 trials; reward probabilities 0.2 and 0.8) and MATLAB code. Appendices cover the theory of model fitting and model comparison, the inversion matrix, a working-memory model and a validation example.

limitations: The ten rules are unnumbered headings. Numbering here follows heading order (rule 1 = s2 to rule 10 = s12; s3 is the worked example, not a rule). The text calls them '10 simple steps (Figure 1)' and cross-refers to 'Step 2' for model design, which matches heading order, but says 'see Step 9' for validating the winning model, which is the eighth heading. The Figure 1 schematic is an image and was not inspected.

Equation 10 is printed as 'BIC = -2 log LL^ + k_m log(T)' with LL^ described as 'the log-likelihood value at the best fitting parameter settings'; read literally this takes the log of a log-likelihood (Appendix Equation 18 has the same form). The repository computes BIC = k log(T) + 2 NegLL, that is -2 times the maximised log-likelihood plus k log T.
Box 1 states that the initial values Q_0^k are zero; the repository's simulate and likelihood functions for Models 3 and 5 initialise Q = [0.5 0.5]. Box 6 states Q_1 = 0.5 for its own simulation.
Equation 3 is printed for 'the value of option k' without restricting the update to the chosen option; the repository updates only the chosen option.
Equation 2 gives no rule for the first trial; the repository uses p = [0.5 0.5] when there is no previous trial.

Exp(10) and Exp(1) are not defined as rate or mean in the paper; the repository draws exprnd(10) and 1+exprnd(1), and MATLAB documentation (mathworks.com/help/stats/exprnd.html, opened 2026-10-31) defines the argument of exprnd as the mean.
Box 4 calls beta the 'softmax temperature', whereas Box 1 defines beta as the inverse temperature.
Box 1 says that with alpha_c = 1 the choice-kernel model is 'very similar to model 2 (win-stay-lose-shift)'; the choice kernel as printed does not use reward, so this sentence needs care in teaching.

Model comparison and model recovery in the examples are in-sample (BIC on the fitted data); cross-validation on held-out data is mentioned only as an alternative. The paper gives no held-out evaluation protocol.

Equations were transcribed from the MathML in the JATS XML; the typeset PDF was not compared. Figure images were not viewed; confusion-matrix values come from the matrices hard-coded in Figure5_both.m.
The README calls the paper 'Ten Simple Rules for Computational Modeling of Psychological Data', which differs from the published title.
